name: Adults
theme: A guided course for adults: the faith made plain, and what to do with it

units.title: Knowing God
units.eq: Is it reasonable to believe, and who is the God Christians believe in?

lessons.title: The question of God
lessons.idea: Almost every culture asks where the world came from and what it is for. The Church holds that reason can reach God as the source of all things, and that this natural knowledge is a doorway to what God has revealed, not a substitute for it.
lessons.question: What experiences (wonder, loss, love, guilt) have made you ask whether God is real?
lessons.activity: Write the two strongest reasons you have heard for belief and for unbelief. Swap with a partner and answer each in a sentence, without arguing, only clarifying. Then name which reason you find most moving, and why.
teach: Reason can know that God exists: “by the natural light of human reason” (CCC 36; Romans 1:19–20; Vatican I). The Church claims this as a possibility open to every person, not a proof that forces belief, and she does not claim reason alone reaches the Trinity or the Gospel.

The classical paths start from the world (motion, cause, contingency, order; Aquinas’ five ways, CCC 34) and from the person (conscience, the longing for truth, goodness and beauty; CCC 33). Each leads to the conclusion that there is a source of all that is, which “all call God.”

Honest limits: these are arguments for a first cause, not the God who calls us by name. Revelation completes what reason begins (CCC 50–53). Faith is not against reason but “goes beyond” it (CCC 156–159).
Take objections seriously: the problem of evil, the success of science, religious diversity and the hiddenness of God. A good answer names the strongest version of the objection before replying.
talk: Where does your own desire for something “more” show up?
Which objections to belief do you find hardest, and why?
What would it take to move from “I think there might be a God” to trusting him?
quiz: What does the Church teach about reason and God?|Only faith can know God and reason is useless|Reason can say nothing about God|Reason can reach God as the source of all things, though faith goes further|God can only be known by feeling|2|CCC 36 teaches that God can be known with certainty by reason from creation.

Which is the better description of faith?|Obedience to rules|Believing without any reason|A free and reasonable trust in God who reveals himself|A feeling of certainty|2|Faith is a personal adherence to God and assent to his truth (CCC 150, 154-155).

Is doubt always a sign of unbelief?|No, it can be a step toward deeper faith if it keeps asking|Yes, always|Only for the uneducated|Only in teenagers|0|Doubt held with honesty and prayer can lead to a stronger faith.
lessons.life: This week, spend ten quiet minutes outside without your phone. Notice what you see, then thank the Creator or, if you are unsure, simply say: “If you are there, show me.”
lessons.saint: Augustine of Hippo: he searched for truth for years before writing, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “Arguments for God are meant to force belief.”
lessons.mem: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (Augustine)
lessons.hook: Ask the group to write, privately, the question about God they would most like answered. Collect them anonymously and read two aloud.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state, in two sentences, one reason reason can point to God and one limit of that reasoning.

lessons.title: One God in three Persons
lessons.idea: Christians believe in one God who is a communion of three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is not a puzzle to solve but the heart of the faith: God is love, and love is shared.
lessons.question: Why does it matter that God is one and also a communion of Persons?
lessons.activity: Take the usual analogies (shamrock, water, sun) and name exactly where each one fails, using the errors of Arius, Sabellius and tritheism as a guide. Then write one sentence about the Trinity that is true and does not fall into any of those errors.
teach: The Trinity is a mystery in the strict sense: a truth we could not know unless God revealed it (CCC 237). It is not a contradiction. We say one God (one divine nature) in three Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), really distinct, equal and eternal (CCC 253–256).

The Church’s language came from the New Testament’s witness (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1–14; 2 Corinthians 13:13) and was fixed at Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381) and later councils to exclude errors: Arius (the Son is a creature), Sabellius or modalism (one God wearing three masks), and tritheism (three gods).

“God is love” (1 John 4:8). If God were a single solitary Person, love would be something God does only after creating. In the Trinity, love is eternal: the Father gives himself wholly to the Son, the Son returns it, and that love is the Holy Spirit (CCC 221).

Every analogy limps (shamrock, water, sun). Use them to name where they fail: the shamrock suggests parts, water suggests modes. The right response to the mystery is worship and the Sign of the Cross, a creed in a gesture (CCC 232–237).
talk: If God is love by nature, what does the Trinity say about why anything exists?
How does knowing God as Father change prayer?
Which Person of the Trinity do you find easiest to pray to? Hardest?
quiz: What does the Church mean by “mystery” when it speaks of the Trinity?|Something nonsensical|A story|A truth we could not know unless God revealed it|A secret for priests|2|CCC 237: the Trinity is the central mystery of faith.
Which description is an error?|The Spirit proceeds from the Father|The Son is begotten of the Father|Three Persons in one God|One God, three masks worn in turn|3|That error is called modalism.
What makes the Persons distinct?|Their power|Their names only|Their relations to one another|Their age|2|The Father, Son and Spirit are distinguished by their relations (CCC 254).
lessons.life: Pray the Sign of the Cross slowly this week, once each morning, thinking of each Person as you say the name.
lessons.saint: Patrick of Ireland: tradition says he used the shamrock to teach the Trinity; the real treasure is his prayer, “Christ with me, Christ before me.”
misc: “The Father is God, the Son is half-God.”
lessons.mem: “Go and make disciples… baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Ask the group to draw the Trinity in 30 seconds, then compare drawings. Which pictures help? Which mislead?
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain why the Trinity is not three gods and not one God in three masks.

lessons.title: Jesus: who do you say he is?
lessons.idea: Jesus is the Son of God made man. He is not merely a great teacher: he claims to forgive sins, to be Lord of the Sabbath and one with the Father, and he rose from the dead. The question he asks, “Who do you say that I am?”, is put to every generation.
lessons.question: Who do you actually think Jesus is, and where did that come from?
lessons.activity: Read Mark 2:1–12 aloud. List every claim the passage makes about who Jesus is, directly or indirectly, and what reaction each claim causes. Decide what you would have had to believe about him to be offended, and what to believe to be amazed.
teach: The Church confesses that Jesus is true God and true man: one divine Person with two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation (Chalcedon, 451; CCC 464–469). He has a human body, soul, mind and will.

The Gospels show claims that go beyond a teacher: forgiving sins (Mark 2:5–7), lordship over the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The Jewish listeners understood what he claimed (John 10:33).

C. S. Lewis’ trilemma (liar, lunatic or Lord) is useful but incomplete; a fair account also considers legend and the reliability of the sources (see Session 2.1). The best case rests on the Gospels, the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15) and the faith of the first community, not on a single argument.

Titles carry meaning: Messiah (anointed king), Son of God, Son of Man (Daniel 7), Lord (the divine name in the Greek Old Testament) (CCC 436–451). Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27–30) is the hinge of the Gospels.
talk: Why do people often want Jesus to be only a teacher?
What changes in your life if he is only a good man? What changes if he is Lord?
Which title (Messiah, Son of God, Lord) speaks to you most right now?
quiz: What did the Council of Chalcedon teach?|Jesus became God at his baptism|Jesus had a divine mind in a human body|Jesus is one Person in two natures, divine and human|Jesus only seemed to be human|2|CCC 467.
Which Gospel passage shows Jesus claiming to forgive sins?|Mark 8:27|John 21|Luke 2:1|Mark 2:1-12|3|Only God can forgive sins, which is why the scribes object.
What does “incarnation” mean?|Man became divine|God speaks through a prophet|Christ had no body|God became man|3|CCC 461.
lessons.life: Read one chapter of Mark this week in one sitting, as if you had never read it, asking one question: what does this tell me about who he is?
lessons.saint: Peter: he answered, “You are the Christ,” then denied him, then was forgiven; his whole story is an answer to Jesus’ question.
misc: “Jesus is just a great moral teacher.”
lessons.mem: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If a friend asked who Jesus is, what would you say in one sentence?” Collect answers, then read Mark 8:27–30.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to list two claims Jesus makes about himself and what follows if they are true.

units.title: Can I trust the Bible and the Church?
units.eq: How does God speak, and who speaks for him today?

lessons.title: How the Bible came to be
lessons.idea: The Bible is a library of 73 books written over about a thousand years. Catholics believe God is its author and that human authors wrote in their own style and time. The Church recognized which books belong and reads them as one story that leads to Christ.
lessons.question: What do you assume about the Bible, and where did you get that idea?
lessons.activity: Compare the healing of the paralytic in Mark 2:1–12 and Luke 5:17–26. List what the two share and what differs, and say what each author seems to want you to notice. Then read the same story in Matthew 9:1–8 and ask what the differences teach about how the Gospels were written.
teach: The Bible is a library of 73 books (46 Old Testament, 27 New) written over about a thousand years in many forms: history, law, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, gospel, letter, apocalypse. God is the author and human writers were “true authors” who used their own powers (CCC 105–107).

Inspiration means Scripture teaches “without error the truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation” (CCC 107; Dei Verbum 11). That does not make every verse a lesson in science or modern history. Ask what the author intended, given the form and the time (CCC 109–110).

Three rules for reading (CCC 112–114): attend to the unity of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and keep the coherence of the faith in view (the analogy of faith). Add the four senses: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical (CCC 115–117).

The canon: the Church, in the fourth century (Hippo 393, Carthage 397; confirmed by Pope Innocent I), recognized which books were inspired. Catholics and Orthodox keep seven Old Testament books (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees) that were in the Greek Bible of the early Church; many Protestants omit them.
talk: What is the difference between asking “did this happen?” and “what is this passage teaching?”
Why does it matter that the Church read the Bible before it was written down in one book?
What part of Scripture have you never read? What is stopping you?
quiz: Who is the author of Scripture, according to the Church?|God, who inspired the human authors|Only human beings|Nobody knows|The Church councils|0|CCC 105-106.
How many books are in the Catholic Bible?|66|73|100|81|1|46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New (CCC 120).

Which is NOT one of the Church’s three criteria for interpreting Scripture?|Each person’s private feeling alone|The living Tradition of the Church|The analogy of faith|The unity of the whole of Scripture|0|CCC 112-114.
lessons.life: Read the Mass readings each day this week using the Readings page and write one sentence on what stood out.
lessons.saint: Jerome: he spent decades translating Scripture into Latin and wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”
misc: “The Church invented the Bible to control people.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a hand-copied page and a printed page. Ask how we can trust that an ancient text has been passed on well.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain inspiration, the canon and one way to read a hard passage well.

lessons.title: Tradition and the teaching authority
lessons.idea: Jesus did not write a book; he formed a community and sent it. The apostles handed on what they had received in preaching and worship before the New Testament was complete. Catholics believe Christ keeps the Church faithful in teaching through the pope and bishops.
lessons.question: Why do you think many people trust a book more than a community, or the reverse?
lessons.activity: Read 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 2 Timothy 2:2, and trace the chain of teaching they describe from Paul to Timothy to others. Draw it as a diagram, then label where Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium appear. Write one sentence on what would go wrong if any one were removed.
teach: Jesus did not write a book; he formed a community and sent it (Matthew 28:19–20). The apostles handed on what they received by preaching and worship before and alongside the New Testament (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 2 Timothy 2:2). This living handing-on is Tradition (CCC 75–79).

Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source and form one deposit of faith (CCC 80–82). Tradition is not a second book of extra teachings; it is the Church’s living memory of the Gospel in her teaching, worship and life, and it is how the Church knows what Scripture means and which books belong.

The Magisterium, the bishops with the Pope, interprets the Word of God authentically. It is not above the Word but serves it, teaching “only what has been handed on” (CCC 85–87). The Spirit’s promise (John 16:12–13) is that the Church will be guided into all truth.

Infallibility is narrow: the Pope teaching definitively as pastor of all on faith or morals, or the bishops with him doing the same, are preserved from error (CCC 889–892). It does not make every statement of a pope infallible, nor does it mean the Pope is sinless. Doctrine develops (deepens) without contradicting what came before.
talk: What do you gain from a Church that teaches with authority? What do you find hard?
What is the difference between Tradition and traditions (customs)?
How does the idea of apostolic succession answer the question “who decides?”
quiz: What is the “deposit of faith”?|The truth of revelation entrusted to the Church|The Church’s buildings|Money kept in a bank|A list of rules|0|CCC 84.
Infallibility means the pope…|Never sins|Can invent new doctrine|Is right about science|Cannot err when defining a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church|3|CCC 891.
What is apostolic succession?|Bishops receiving authority in unbroken line from the apostles|Popes choosing their heirs|Using the same Bible|Priests wearing the same vestments|0|CCC 861-862.
lessons.life: Choose one teaching of the Church you find hard. Read the Catechism paragraph on it and, before you decide, read the reasons the Church gives.
lessons.saint: Irenaeus of Lyons: he defended the faith against false teachers by pointing to the churches founded by the apostles and the bishops who followed them.
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know what your grandparents were like if you never met them?” Link to oral and written handing-on.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe how Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together.

lessons.title: Why the Church? Why not just Jesus?
lessons.idea: Many say, “I like Jesus but not the Church.” The Church teaches that Christ founded a visible community and that he is present in it, the Body of Christ. The Church is made of sinners and saints, and her sins are real; but she is also where we receive the sacraments and hear the Gospel.
lessons.question: What hurt, scandal or disappointment has shaped how you think about the Church?
lessons.activity: Read Acts 2:42–47 and list the four things the first believers “devoted themselves to.” For each one, write whether your life already includes it, and one small step to add it. Then write a candid sentence about what bothers you most about the Church and one thing she has given you.
teach: Christ founded a visible community: he chose the Twelve, gave Peter the keys (Matthew 16:18–19), instituted the Eucharist and sent the apostles with authority to teach, baptize and forgive sins (Matthew 28:19; John 20:21–23; CCC 551–553, 765).

The Church is both holy and made of sinners (CCC 827). She is holy in her Head and in her means of grace, and always in need of purification. The scandals are real; the saints show the same Church can also produce astonishing holiness.

The Church is described as the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 1:22–23), the People of God, and the Temple of the Spirit (CCC 781–801). “I like Jesus but not the Church” misses that Jesus chose to be present to us through a body: Word, sacraments and a community.
Acts 2:42–47 shows the pattern: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers. A fair test of whether you are part of the Church is whether you have those four.
talk: What is the difference between the Church’s teaching and the failings of her members?
What would you miss if the Church were not there?
What community of faith do you actually belong to right now?
quiz: What are the four marks of the Church?|One, holy, catholic, apostolic|Rome, Paris, Jerusalem, Antioch|Old, big, rich, strict|Faith, hope, love, mercy|0|CCC 811.
Is the Church free of sin?|Her members sin, though she is holy in Christ and her sacraments|No one is holy|Yes, all members are sinless|Only the clergy sin|0|CCC 827.
What did the first Christians devote themselves to?|Silence|Debate|Teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers|Wealth and travel|2|Acts 2:42.
lessons.life: Go to Mass this week, even one weekday, and arrive early. Pray for the person who first taught you about God.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: she loved the Church while telling popes and bishops hard truths. “Be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire.”
lessons.mem: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” (Matthew 18:20)
lessons.hook: Poll: “Have you ever said ‘I like Jesus but not the Church’? What makes you say it?” Listen without defending.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to give two reasons the Church is more than an institution and one honest struggle.

units.title: Prayer: learning to talk with God
units.eq: How do I pray when it feels empty?

lessons.title: What prayer is and why it is hard
lessons.idea: Prayer is the raising of the mind and heart to God. It is a relationship, not a performance. Dryness, distraction and doubt are normal, and the saints describe them too. The way through is to keep showing up with honesty.
lessons.question: What gets in the way of your prayer: time, boredom, doubt, guilt, noise?
lessons.activity: Try ten minutes of silent prayer with no phone. After, write one honest sentence about what happened, even if it is “I was bored.” Then choose one practice from the lesson (a psalm, the Jesus Prayer, a Gospel scene) and commit to it for one week.
teach: Prayer is “the raising of one’s mind and heart to God” (CCC 2559). It is a relationship: God thirsts for us first (CCC 2560), and prayer is our answer. The Psalms and the Our Father are the Church’s school of prayer (CCC 2585–2589, 2759–2761).

Dryness, distraction and doubt are normal and not a sign of failure (CCC 2726–2733). Distraction is not sin; it becomes a problem only when we cling to it. Acedia, a kind of spiritual laziness, is the great enemy of persevering prayer (CCC 2733).

Practical help: choose a time and place; start with a short, fixed amount (ten minutes); use Scripture, a psalm or the Jesus Prayer to hold your attention; keep a note of what you notice. Jesus’ own advice: pray in secret and without piling up words (Matthew 6:5–8).

The Church names five forms (blessing/adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise) and three expressions (vocal, meditation, contemplation) (CCC 2626–2643, 2700–2724). Most beginners need only start with one.
talk: When have you felt closest to God in prayer? What was different?
What would you say to God if you were completely honest?
How is prayer different from meditating or clearing your mind?
quiz: What is prayer?|A way to get what we want|The raising of the mind and heart to God|A technique to relax|Reciting words|1|CCC 2559.
Which is one of the five forms of prayer?|Rituals|Thanksgiving|Argument|Silence only|1|CCC 2626-2643.
What should you do when prayer feels dry?|Skip it|Keep praying, keep it simple, and be honest|Pray longer words|Give up until you feel it|1|CCC 2729.
lessons.life: Set an alarm for a daily five-minute prayer for seven days. Same time, same place, same short routine.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: she called prayer “a surge of the heart” and kept faith through years of darkness.
misc: “If prayer feels dry, God is absent.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Set a ten-second silence. Ask: “What was your mind doing?” Name the experience of distraction.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name one obstacle in their prayer and one remedy they will try.

lessons.title: Praying with Scripture: lectio divina
lessons.idea: Lectio divina is a slow, prayerful reading of a short passage in four movements: read (lectio), reflect (meditatio), respond (oratio), rest (contemplatio). It lets God’s word become a conversation.
lessons.question: Which passage of Scripture has ever “spoken” to you?
lessons.activity: Practice lectio divina on Luke 24:13–35 together, or alone. After each step, write a few words. Share one thing from the oratio step (your response to God). Plan three more mornings this week using the next day’s Mass reading.
teach: Lectio divina is the Church’s ancient way of praying with Scripture: read (lectio), reflect (meditatio), respond (oratio), rest (contemplatio), and then act (actio) (CCC 2705–2708). It comes from the Fathers and monasteries (Origen, Ambrose, Benedict), and Dei Verbum 25 urges all the faithful to it.

The key is slowness: read a short passage aloud, stop at the word or phrase that stands out, ask what God is saying to you through it, answer him in your own words, then be still. You are not trying to finish a text but to meet a Person.

Scripture is the place God speaks: “the word of God is living and active” (Hebrews 4:12; Psalm 119:105). The Emmaus story (Luke 24:13–35) shows the pattern: Jesus explains the Scriptures and the disciples’ hearts burn within them; they recognize him in the breaking of bread.

Keep it ordered: pray with the Church’s readings (the Mass of the day is a good source), read with the Church’s mind (see Session 2.1), and test your insights with a wise guide. Prayer with Scripture is meant to lead to Christ and to love of neighbor.
talk: What phrase stood out to you? Why do you think?
How is this different from studying the passage?
How could you do this with the Mass readings each morning?
quiz: What are the four steps of lectio divina?|Study, memorize, quote, teach|Read, reflect, respond, rest|Ask, seek, knock, wait|Sing, kneel, stand, sit|1|The traditional movements.
Whom did Jesus walk with on the road to Emmaus?|Mary and Joseph|Two disciples|The apostles|Peter alone|1|Luke 24:13.
Why pray with Scripture?|To impress others|To hear God’s word as addressed to me|To avoid thinking|To replace the Mass|1|CCC 2653.
lessons.life: Pray with the Sunday Gospel before Mass this week: read it Monday, linger on one line each day.
lessons.saint: Ambrose and Augustine: Augustine famously saw Ambrose reading silently, and later himself heard “take and read” and opened Romans 13.
lessons.mem: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” (Psalm 119:105)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 23 first fast, then slowly with pauses. Ask what changed.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the four movements of lectio divina and share one word that stood out.

lessons.title: The Mass as prayer
lessons.idea: The Mass is the Church’s greatest prayer. In it Christ’s sacrifice on the cross is made present and we receive him. Praying the Mass means more than watching: it means offering your life with Christ.
lessons.question: What do you usually think about during Mass? What would you like to think about?
lessons.activity: Go through the Order of Mass using Mass mode in the app. At each part, name one thing you could offer to God (a worry, a person, a gift, a failure). Pick the part you most often tune out and plan one way to be present for it next Sunday.
teach: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (CCC 1324). At Mass, Christ’s one sacrifice on the Cross is made present and we are united to it (CCC 1362–1367); we also receive him as food (John 6:51–58). Praying the Mass means offering ourselves with Christ, not only attending.

The shape follows Emmaus: gathering, Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist, sending (CCC 1346–1355). At each step you can offer something: sorrow at the penitential act, attention to the readings, your week at the offertory, your needs at the Prayer of the Faithful, thanksgiving after Communion.

Full, conscious, active participation (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14) is first interior: listening, responding, singing, kneeling, silence. Preparation (reading the Sunday readings in advance, Confession if needed, the fast of one hour) and thanksgiving matter (CCC 1385–1387).
On dry days the Mass still works: it is Christ’s action, not our mood (ex opere operato, CCC 1128), though our faith and attention open us to its fruit.
talk: What do you find hard about Mass? What helps?
How would you explain to a friend why Catholics go every week?
What is something you could offer to God at the offertory?
quiz: The Eucharist is…|A symbol of unity|A meal like others|The source and summit of Christian life|Only a memorial|2|CCC 1324.
The two main parts of the Mass are…|Offering and sermon|The Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist|Entrance and dismissal|Songs and prayers|1|CCC 1346.
What is “active participation”?|Singing loudly|Offering oneself with Christ in prayer and attention|Holding hands|Doing lots of tasks|1|CCC 1368.
lessons.life: Attend Mass once during the week and use Mass mode. Afterwards write the one line you want to carry into the day.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager who called the Eucharist his “highway to heaven” and used his computer skills to share it.
misc: “I get nothing out of it, so it’s pointless.”
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you bring to Mass besides yourself?” Invite one thing to offer this Sunday.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the parts of the Mass and one way to participate more fully.

units.title: Sin, mercy and Confession
units.eq: How do I deal with guilt and failure?

lessons.title: Sin: what it is and what it does
lessons.idea: Sin is an offense against God and a wound to ourselves and others. The Church distinguishes mortal sin (which breaks our friendship with God) from venial sin (which weakens it). Naming sin honestly is the first step toward mercy.
lessons.question: Why is it hard to speak honestly about sin?
lessons.activity: Read Psalm 51 slowly. Underline each action David asks of God (wash, cleanse, create, restore). Write what you would ask for in your own words. Then list three effects of sin (on God, self, others) and one way mercy answers each.
teach: Sin is an offense against God and a wound to ourselves and others (CCC 1849–1851). It is not only breaking rules; it is a failure of love and a lie about who we are. Scripture is honest about it: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

The Church distinguishes mortal sin, which breaks our friendship with God, from venial sin, which wounds it. Mortal sin needs three conditions together: grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1855–1862). Many people worry too much or too little; Confession is the place to sort it out.

Romans 7:15–25 describes the divided heart: “I do not do what I want.” Paul does not despair: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ.” Concupiscence, the inclination to sin that remains after Baptism, is a struggle and not itself a sin (CCC 1264).

Psalm 51 is the model prayer after sin: honest naming (“I know my transgressions”), a plea for mercy and a clean heart, and a promise to teach others. God does not stop at forgiving; he renews (“create in me a clean heart”).
talk: How is guilt different from shame?
Why do you think the Church names specific sins instead of only talking in general?
What is the difference between a mistake and a sin?
quiz: Which is NOT a condition for mortal sin?|Full knowledge|Being caught|Grave matter|Deliberate consent|1|CCC 1857.
Venial sin…|Weakens charity but does not destroy it|Is not really sin|Cuts off grace entirely|Cannot be forgiven|0|CCC 1855.
What is conscience?|Habit|A feeling|The Church’s rules|A judgment of reason that tells us the moral quality of an act|3|CCC 1778.
lessons.life: Spend ten minutes in an examination of conscience this week using the app’s Examination page. Write nothing down; simply notice.
lessons.saint: Augustine: his Confessions show how honest naming of sin can become praise.
misc: “I am too bad to be forgiven.”
lessons.mem: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” (1 John 1:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do people mean when they say ‘that’s not a big deal’? When is that true and false?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to define mortal and venial sin and explain the three conditions for mortal sin.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Confession
lessons.idea: In Confession Christ forgives sins through the priest. The sacrament has four parts: contrition, confession, penance and absolution. It is a meeting with mercy, not a courtroom.
lessons.question: What is your biggest worry about going to Confession?
lessons.activity: Learn the steps of Confession and practice them aloud (not your real sins). Read the parable of the Prodigal Son and notice who runs. Then write a short examination of conscience based on the Ten Commandments, and decide a date for your next Confession.
teach: Christ gave the apostles power to forgive sins on Easter evening (John 20:21–23), and the Church exercises it through bishops and priests acting in the person of Christ (CCC 1441–1445, 1461). The sacrament goes by several names: Penance, Reconciliation, Confession, Conversion.

The parts: contrition (sorrow, with the intent to sin no more), confession (naming sins, grave ones in kind and number), satisfaction (penance), and absolution (CCC 1450–1460, 1480). Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect from fear or shame, and is still enough for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

The seal is absolute: a priest may never reveal anything heard in Confession (CCC 1467). Mortal sin must be confessed before receiving Communion, and everyone who has reached the age of reason must confess grave sin at least once a year (CCC 1457, 2042).

The parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) shows the Father who runs. The sacrament gives more than a feeling: forgiveness of sin, restored grace, peace, and strength to resist (CCC 1468–1470). If it has been years, just say so: “It has been a long time.” The priest will help.
talk: Why did Jesus give the power to forgive sins to men?
What do you think the father in the Prodigal Son parable says about God?
What would make it easier for you to go?
quiz: What are the four parts of Confession?|Contrition, confession, penance, absolution|Confession, counseling, therapy, forgiveness|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving, silence|Sorrow, regret, shame, hope|0|CCC 1450-1460.
Who can forgive sins in the sacrament?|A deacon|A bishop only|A priest, in the person of Christ|Any believer|2|CCC 1461.
The seal of confession means…|The priest may never reveal what was confessed|The sacrament is private|The priest may share it with the bishop|The penitent cannot speak|0|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Schedule a Confession this week. If it has been years, say so; the priest will help you.
lessons.saint: John Vianney: he spent up to sixteen hours a day hearing confessions in a small village in France.
lessons.mem: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” (John 20:23)
lessons.hook: Read the Prodigal Son. Ask: “Who runs? Who waits? What does the father say?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to list the four parts of Confession and answer “Why a priest?”

lessons.title: Receiving mercy and giving it
lessons.idea: Forgiveness is not only something we receive; it is something we are asked to give. Jesus ties the two together in the Our Father. Mercy changes how we treat those who have wronged us.
lessons.question: Who is hardest for you to forgive?
lessons.activity: Write an unsent letter to someone you need to forgive (or to ask forgiveness from). Pray over it. Decide whether to send, to speak, or to leave it with God for now. Then choose one work of mercy to perform this week and do it.
teach: Forgiveness is a gift we receive and a gift we are asked to give: “forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us” (Matthew 6:12–15; CCC 2838–2845). Jesus ties them together and the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35) makes the point sharply.

Forgiving does not mean excusing, forgetting or staying in an unsafe situation (CCC 2843–2845). It means letting go of the claim to repay hurt with hurt, wishing the other well and, where possible, being open to reconciliation. Justice and safety remain important; some wounds need time, counsel and sometimes professional help.

Mercy is more than a feeling: the works of mercy (CCC 2447) are corporal (feeding, clothing, visiting) and spiritual (instructing, counseling, forgiving, bearing wrongs patiently, praying). “Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

The Church’s own history shows both the need and the practice: John Paul II’s apology for sins of the Church’s children in 2000, the witness of Maria Goretti and Maximilian Kolbe, and the forgiveness of Pope John Paul II toward his attacker.
talk: What is the difference between forgiving and trusting again?
Why does Jesus say we are forgiven as we forgive?
Which work of mercy could you do this week?
quiz: What does the Our Father say about forgiveness?|Forgive and forget|Forgive us when we ask|Forgive us as we forgive others|Forgive only the good|2|Matthew 6:12.
Which is a corporal work of mercy?|Visit the sick|Instruct the ignorant|Counsel the doubtful|Pray for the dead|0|CCC 2447.
Forgiveness means…|Letting go of resentment and wishing the other well|Never speaking of it|Pretending nothing happened|Being weak|0|CCC 2843.
lessons.life: Do one work of mercy this week that costs you something: time, money or comfort.
lessons.saint: Maria Goretti: she forgave her attacker as she was dying, and he later repented.
lessons.mem: “Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.” (Our Father)
lessons.hook: Ask silently: “Who is hardest to forgive?” Hold the question; do not share.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain what forgiveness is not and one step toward it.

units.title: The Eucharist and the sacraments
units.eq: What happens in the sacraments, and why do they matter?

lessons.title: What is a sacrament?
lessons.idea: A sacrament is an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies. The seven sacraments carry us from birth to death. They are not magic; they are encounters with Christ in the Church.
lessons.question: Which sacrament do you understand least?
lessons.activity: Make a chart of the seven sacraments with their sign (matter), words (form), minister and what they do. Fill in what you can; look up the rest. Then circle the sacrament you understand least and write two questions about it to ask a priest or catechist.
teach: A sacrament is an outward sign, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, that gives the grace it signifies (CCC 1131). The sign has matter (water, oil, bread, wine), form (words) and a minister. Jesus’ touch in the Gospels (Mark 7:31–37) continues in them (CCC 1115–1116).

There are seven, in three groups: initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), healing (Penance, Anointing of the Sick), and service of communion (Holy Orders, Matrimony) (CCC 1210–1211). Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders can be received only once because they imprint a permanent character (CCC 1121).

They work ex opere operato: by Christ’s action, not by the minister’s holiness (CCC 1127–1128). The fruit depends on our faith and disposition: a gift can be received or refused. Grace is God’s life in us (CCC 1996–2000).

Because God became flesh, he uses matter to give grace. Sacraments are not magic and not mere symbols; they are encounters. Sacramentals (blessings, holy water, medals) are different: instituted by the Church to prepare us for grace (CCC 1667–1673).
talk: Why does Christ use physical things (water, oil, bread, wine)?
Which sacrament has marked your life most?
What is the difference between a sacrament and a sign or symbol?
quiz: How many sacraments are there?|Nine|Twelve|Seven|Five|2|CCC 1113.
Ex opere operato means…|The minister’s holiness gives the effect|It works only if we feel something|It is just a symbol|The sacrament works through Christ’s action|3|CCC 1128.
Which is a sacrament of service?|Confirmation|Baptism|Reconciliation|Matrimony|3|CCC 1534.
lessons.life: Pick one sacrament and learn its words and gestures. Teach it to someone this week.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: his hymns for Corpus Christi (like Tantum Ergo) are still sung.
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Hold up water, oil, bread and a ring. Ask what each is used for and what happens when God uses them.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the seven sacraments with their matter and form.

lessons.title: The Eucharist: real presence
lessons.idea: Catholics believe that after the consecration the bread and wine are truly the Body and Blood of Christ, soul and divinity. This belief rests on John 6, the words at the Last Supper and the faith of the earliest Christians.
lessons.question: What would it mean for your Sunday if Jesus is really present on the altar?
lessons.activity: Read John 6:51–69 and notice who left and why. Read 1 Corinthians 11:27–29: what did Paul think was at stake? Then spend ten minutes in front of the Blessed Sacrament (or read the Pange Lingua / Tantum Ergo) and write what you notice about your own belief.
teach: The Church believes that after the consecration the bread and wine are truly the Body and Blood, soul and divinity of Christ (CCC 1374). The word transubstantiation names the change of substance while the appearances remain (CCC 1376). This is Christ’s own claim: “my flesh is true food” (John 6:55), and many disciples left because of it (John 6:60–66).

The words of institution (Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26) say “This is my body,” not “this represents.” Paul warns that eating unworthily brings judgment on “the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27–29), which only makes sense if it is more than a symbol.

The Fathers taught it from the start: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) calls the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ”; Justin Martyr (c. 155) says it is not common bread. Disputes about how came later; Trent defined the term in 1551.

It leads to reverence: genuflecting, preparation, the one-hour fast, Eucharistic adoration (CCC 1378–1381). Real Presence is also why Communion unites us: “we, though many, are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17).
talk: Why did many disciples leave in John 6?
What does it say about Jesus that he did not soften the teaching?
How do you prepare to receive Communion?
quiz: What happens at the consecration?|The bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood|The bread symbolizes Christ|Christ is remembered|Nothing changes|0|CCC 1376.
Which passage is the “Bread of Life discourse”?|Acts 2|John 6|Luke 24|Matthew 5|1|John 6:22-71.
To receive Communion worthily one must be…|Over 18|In a state of grace|Wealthy|A member of the choir|1|CCC 1385.
lessons.life: Visit a church for ten minutes of Eucharistic adoration this week. Say nothing and let yourself be looked at.
lessons.saint: Pier Giorgio Frassati: a young Italian who went to Mass and adoration daily and served the poor, died at 24 of polio.
lessons.mem: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” (John 6:68)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:60–69. Ask: “Why did many leave? Why did Peter stay?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain transubstantiation in plain words and cite two texts.

lessons.title: Baptism, Confirmation and living them
lessons.idea: Baptism makes us children of God and members of the Church; Confirmation seals us with the Spirit for mission. For adults, these are not just past events but a vocation: live as the baptized.
lessons.question: Do you think of yourself as a priest, prophet and king by baptism? What would that mean?
lessons.activity: Go through the baptismal promises. Which would you find hardest to say today? Write a personal renewal of them in your own words. Then find out whether you are confirmed and, if not, what your parish offers for adults.
teach: Baptism removes original sin and all personal sin, gives new birth as a child of God, incorporates us into Christ and the Church, and imprints a permanent mark (CCC 1262–1274; Romans 6:3–11; John 3:5). Its sign is water and the Trinitarian words; anyone can baptize in an emergency.

The baptismal promises are renewed at every Easter Vigil: renouncing sin and the devil and professing the Creed. For an adult, Baptism is not only a past event but a vocation to live as a “priest, prophet and king” (CCC 897–913).

Confirmation completes Baptism: sealing with the Holy Spirit by anointing with chrism and the words “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” It deepens baptismal grace and equips for witness (CCC 1285, 1302–1305; Acts 8:14–17). The seven gifts (Isaiah 11:2) are given; the fruits (Galatians 5:22–23) are what they produce.

If you were baptized but never confirmed, you can be: ask your parish. If you were not baptized, RCIA (the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults) is the path. Either way, these sacraments are not graduations but beginnings.
talk: If you were baptized as an infant, how has that faith become your own?
What is one gift of the Holy Spirit you most need now?
What does being a “priestly people” mean for a lay person at work?
quiz: Baptism does…|Remove original and personal sins and give new life|Only mark someone as Catholic|Make no change|Give a name|0|CCC 1263.
Confirmation…|Replaces Baptism|Seals us with the Holy Spirit|Is optional for everyone|Is just a graduation|1|CCC 1303.

The seven gifts of the Spirit include…|Prudence, justice, temperance|Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord|Patience, kindness, goodness|Faith, hope, love|1|Isaiah 11:2.
lessons.life: Renew your baptismal promises this week, kneeling at home before a crucifix or holy water.
lessons.saint: Philip Neri: the joyful “apostle of Rome” who gathered young people for prayer, humor and service.
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Romans 6:3)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would change if you took your baptism as seriously as a wedding?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name what Baptism and Confirmation do and one concrete way to live them.

units.title: Love, sexuality and chastity
units.eq: What does it mean to love?

lessons.title: Made for love
lessons.idea: God made us male and female in his image, for communion. Our bodies and sexuality are good and are meant to express self-gift. Chastity is the virtue that integrates sexuality in the person, so that love is real.
lessons.question: What messages about love and sex did you absorb growing up, and which do you now doubt?
lessons.activity: Write down what popular culture says about love and sex, then what you think the Church says. Compare. Choose one phrase from the lesson (the body is good; love is gift of self; chastity builds freedom) and write what it would change in your relationships.
teach: God made us male and female in his image (Genesis 1:27), and the body is good: it expresses the person (CCC 355–357, 2331–2336). Sexuality is for love and life; it is a language of self-giving that tells the truth only when it is total, faithful and open to life (CCC 2360–2365).

Love is willing the good of the other (CCC 1766; Aquinas). The Song of Solomon (8:6–7) shows its strength: “love is strong as death.” The Church’s teaching on chastity is not hatred of the body but a protection of persons from being used (CCC 2337–2347).

Chastity is the integration of sexuality within the whole person, and everyone is called to it according to their state: engaged, married, single or consecrated (CCC 2348–2350). It is a virtue to be built, with grace and friends, and not simply a list of prohibitions.
Be honest: many people have been hurt by sexual abuse, by shame, or by others’ choices. The Church’s teaching comes with mercy: Confession and accompaniment are always available (CCC 2352–2356).
talk: What is the difference between love and use?
How do you think the culture shapes how young adults think about relationships?
How is chastity different from repression?
quiz: Chastity is…|The same as celibacy|Hatred of the body|The successful integration of sexuality within the person|Only for single people|2|CCC 2337.
What does “image of God” mean for the body?|Persons are body and soul, and the body expresses the person|The soul is a prisoner|The body is irrelevant|Sex is bad|0|CCC 362-364.
Who is called to chastity?|Only unmarried people|Everyone, according to their state of life|Only the young|Only priests|1|CCC 2348.
lessons.life: Take a week off one media habit that shapes your view of love and sex (a feed, a show, a playlist). Notice what changes.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: his talks on the theology of the body began as Wednesday audiences, and he gave his life to teaching what love means.
misc: “The Church thinks the body is bad.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image… male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do films and songs say love is? What do they leave out?” Take a few answers.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state what the Church means by love and what gift of self requires.

lessons.title: Dating, discernment and boundaries
lessons.idea: Dating is a time to get to know someone with a view to a possible marriage, not only enjoyment. Christian dating asks for honesty, respect for the other person’s freedom and chastity, and prayer.
lessons.question: What would you want a person you date to know about your values before the relationship starts?
lessons.activity: Draft a short list of the qualities you are looking for in a spouse (or the kind of friend and partner you want to be) and a short list of boundaries you would set, with a reason for each. Share one with a trusted friend or mentor for honest feedback.
teach: Dating is a time of discernment: it is meant to help two people know whether they are called to marriage (CCC 1632, 2350). Seek character before chemistry: faith, honesty, kindness, how they treat family and strangers, how they handle conflict.

Boundaries protect love: decide beforehand, in prayer and with a friend, what physical limits fit the stage of the relationship. The Church asks engaged and dating couples to live chastity, because sexual union belongs to the covenant of marriage (CCC 2350–2351, 2390).

Healthy signs: freedom, respect for no, being known without fear, friends and family who are glad. Red flags: control, isolation, pressure, secrecy, escalating guilt. If you feel afraid, seek help; abuse is never a sign of love.

Proverbs 4:23: “Guard your heart.” Practical help: group settings, a friend who will be honest, limiting late nights alone, regular Mass and Confession, and being open about the question “Where is this going?”
talk: What makes it hard to date in a way that matches your faith?
How can you speak honestly about your values without judging?
How do you handle breakups and rejection?
quiz: What does the Church say about sex before marriage?|It is permitted when in love|It is neutral|It is required to test compatibility|It is contrary to the total self-gift of marriage|3|CCC 2353.
Why wait?|Because of fear|For no reason|Because the body’s language of total self-gift needs a total, public and permanent commitment|It is just a rule|2|CCC 2361-2362.
If someone struggles with sexual sin, the Church offers…|Exclusion|Only condemnation|Silence|Mercy and practical help|3|CCC 2359.
lessons.life: If you are dating, talk about your plans for chastity and marriage this week. If you are single, write a prayer for your future spouse or your vocation.
lessons.saint: Chiara Luce Badano: a joyful teenager who offered her illness to God and died at 18; she is a model of young love for Christ.
lessons.mem: “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” (Proverbs 4:23)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What makes a relationship healthy? What are red flags?” List both columns.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to draft three boundaries and one question for discernment.

lessons.title: Pornography, healing and freedom
lessons.idea: Pornography is widespread and harmful. The Church speaks of it plainly because it wounds the dignity of persons, but she speaks of mercy even more. Healing is possible with grace, honesty, community and professional help.
lessons.question: What do you think pornography teaches about people? About yourself?
lessons.activity: Make a written plan for freedom: one step for your phone and devices, one for community (a person you will tell), one for prayer and the sacraments, and one for care of your body and sleep. If this is not your struggle, write a plan to support a friend who is struggling, without shame.
teach: Pornography harms: it uses persons as objects, distorts desire, can become compulsive, and wounds relationships (CCC 2354). The Church calls it a grave offense because it damages the dignity of those who make and view it. Naming it clearly is part of freedom.

The way out is grace and practice. “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). There is “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). God provides “a way out” of temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13). Shame keeps people hiding; mercy brings them into the light.

Practical steps: tell a trusted person, use filters and accountability, set up your phone and room to remove easy access, go to Confession (as often as needed), pray the Our Father in temptation, find a replacement activity, and seek counseling when the habit is compulsive. Relapse is not the end.
For those harmed by others’ use (spouses, partners), the Church offers compassion and resources. Seek help from a priest or a counselor trained in this area.
talk: What small steps help you resist temptation?
Who can you tell? What stops you?
How does mercy change the way you see yourself?
quiz: The Church treats pornography as…|A harmless habit|A grave offense against dignity|A private matter|A cultural issue|1|CCC 2354.
Which response is most Christian toward someone who struggles?|Shame|Condemnation|Mercy and practical help|Silence|2|John 8:11.
What is a sign of progress?|Hiding|Never failing|Counting days|Getting up again and again with God’s help|3|The saints persevere in humility.
lessons.life: Take one practical step this week: install a filter, tell a friend or priest, or schedule a counselor.
lessons.saint: Augustine: he struggled with lust for years and prayed, “Give me chastity, but not yet.” God’s grace won.
misc: “Everyone does it, so it does no harm.”
“I can fix this entirely on my own.”
lessons.mem: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)
lessons.hook: Say plainly that this is a topic where shame can silence people, and that the focus is on freedom and healing, not blame.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name two practical steps toward freedom (accountability, filters, confession, counsel).

units.title: Vocation: what is God asking of me?
units.eq: How do I discern my life’s call?

lessons.title: Every person is called
lessons.idea: Vocation means “call.” God calls every person first to holiness and then to a particular way of living it: marriage, priesthood or consecrated life, or single life given to God. Discernment is a long conversation, not a sudden revelation.
lessons.question: What do you think you want from life? What might God want?
lessons.activity: Make three columns: gifts (what you do well), joys (what gives you life), needs (what the world around you lacks). Fill each with at least five items and look for overlap. Share with a mentor, and list two next steps in discernment (a conversation, a retreat, a trial of service).
teach: Every person is called first to holiness (CCC 825, 2013; Lumen Gentium 40) and then to a particular way of living it: marriage, priesthood and diaconate, consecrated life, or single life given to God (CCC 897–933, 1877–1879). “Vocation” comes from the Latin for “call”; God calls by name (Samuel, 1 Samuel 3; Andrew and John, John 1:35–39).

Discernment is not guessing a hidden plan. It is listening in prayer, knowing your gifts and desires, taking advice from people who know you, and watching where peace and fruit appear. Ignatius taught attention to consolation and desolation, and to testing decisions over time (CCC 2690).

God’s will for you is usually not a puzzle with one right answer to be missed. It is a call to love, and many paths can be faithful. The risk is not “choosing wrong” but never choosing, or choosing from fear.
The Church needs all vocations: parents, priests, religious, single people who serve. Pray for vocations and ask someone whose life you admire how they knew.
talk: What are your gifts? Ask a friend for their answer.
How do you tell the difference between God’s call and your fear?
What is the next faithful step?
quiz: Who is called to holiness?|Only priests|Only saints|Only monastics|Every Christian|3|CCC 2013.
Vocation means…|Education|Hobby|Career|Call|3|Latin vocare.
Discernment involves…|Prayer, gifts, advice and circumstances|Doing what is easiest|Rolling dice|Waiting for a sign in the sky|0|Ignatian discernment.
lessons.life: Ask one person who knows you well: “Where do you see God using me?” Write down the answer.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Loyola: his conversion began when a cannonball shattered his leg. His Spiritual Exercises teach discernment.
misc: “If I choose wrong, I ruin my life.”
lessons.mem: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where have you felt most alive? Where do you feel you are most useful?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the universal call to holiness and one step in discernment.

lessons.title: Marriage and family
lessons.idea: Marriage is a covenant of love between a man and a woman, ordered to their good and to the procreation and education of children. It is a sacrament: a path to holiness and a sign of Christ’s love for the Church.
lessons.question: What do you hope for in a marriage? What worries you?
lessons.activity: Write what you hope your future home would be like: what you would pray, how you would argue, what you would give up. If you are married or engaged, write a one-page prayer for your spouse. Read Ephesians 5:21–33 and underline the verbs that apply to both husbands and wives.
teach: Marriage is a covenant between a baptized man and woman, a lifelong partnership ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children (CCC 1601; Genesis 2:18–24; Mark 10:6–9). The couple confers the sacrament on each other; the priest or deacon witnesses (CCC 1623).

Its essential properties are unity and indissolubility (CCC 1638–1640). Christ raised it to a sacrament as a sign of his love for the Church: “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church” (Ephesians 5:21–33). Mutual submission “out of reverence for Christ” precedes the specific advice; love is sacrificial on both sides.

Consent makes marriage; freedom, maturity and intention to be faithful, permanent and open to children are required (CCC 1625–1632). The Church can declare that a marriage never existed, an annulment, when a defect in consent or form was present (CCC 1629); it is not Catholic divorce.

Preparation matters: marriage preparation, honest talk about money, children, faith and conflict, and a habit of prayer. Families are “domestic churches” (CCC 1655–1658). Natural Family Planning is the Church’s approved way to space births (CCC 2366–2371).
talk: What makes a marriage last, beyond feelings?
How can an unmarried person prepare for marriage now?
What does the family have to do with the Church?
quiz: The ministers of the sacrament of marriage are…|The priest|The parents|The witnesses|The couple|3|CCC 1623.
Marriage by nature is…|Permanent, faithful and open to children|Temporary and flexible|Optional|A contract only|0|CCC 1643.
An annulment declares…|The couple is free to date|The marriage failed|The children illegitimate|The marriage was never valid|3|CCC 1629.
lessons.life: Pray for the marriages you know. Offer to help a couple or a family in a concrete way (a meal, babysitting).
lessons.saint: Louis and Zélie Martin: parents of Thérèse of Lisieux, canonized together as a married couple.
misc: “Marriage is a contract renewable at will.”
lessons.mem: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Mark 10:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you most want your future family to be like?” Write three words.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the four goods of marriage and what preparing for it requires now.

lessons.title: Priesthood, religious life and single life
lessons.idea: Some are called to give their whole lives to God as priests or consecrated persons; others to a single life of service. Each is a gift to the Church and a way of loving.
lessons.question: What stops you from imagining a call to priesthood or consecrated life?
lessons.activity: Read about one religious order or diocesan seminary and write three things that surprised you. Visit, call or email a vocation director if you can. If you are not considering these paths, write a note of thanks to a priest or religious who has helped you.
teach: Holy Orders configures a man to Christ the head and shepherd to serve the Church as bishop, priest or deacon (CCC 1536–1600). The ministerial priesthood is for others: to teach, sanctify and govern, and above all to celebrate the Eucharist and Confession in the person of Christ (CCC 1548–1553).

Consecrated life lives the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience (CCC 914–933). It takes many forms: monks and nuns, religious sisters and brothers, secular institutes, consecrated virgins. The Church esteems it as a special sign of the Kingdom (CCC 1619–1620) while teaching that marriage is also a sacrament and a real path to holiness; the point is not rivalry but that each state shows something of Christ’s love.

Celibacy for the Kingdom is a gift, a way of loving with an undivided heart (Matthew 19:10–12; 1 Corinthians 7:32–35). It is not a loss to be endured but a love to be lived, and it needs community, prayer and friendship to be lived well.

Single life lived in love, service and prayer is a genuine vocation, not a waiting room. Many single people serve family, parish, the poor and their work in ways that others cannot. Ask: “How can I give myself away?”
talk: Why is celibacy a gift and not a loss?
What would you do if you discovered a calling you did not expect?
How can you support priests and religious?
quiz: The evangelical counsels are…|Faith, hope, love|Wisdom, courage, justice|Poverty, chastity, obedience|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving|2|CCC 915.
Is consecrated life “higher” than marriage?|No one can say|It depends on income|It is a different vocation; both lead to holiness|Yes, always|2|CCC 1620.
Who can be ordained a priest?|Any baptized Catholic|Only the old|Anyone who studies|A baptized man called by God and the Church|3|CCC 1577.
lessons.life: Pray for vocations and ask a priest or religious how they knew their call.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi: he left a rich merchant’s life to follow Christ in poverty and founded the Franciscans.
lessons.mem: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” (Matthew 4:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you give your life to? What would you need to let go?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe celibacy as a gift and how single people can live a vocation.

units.title: Work, money and the world
units.eq: How does faith shape the way I live in the world?

lessons.title: Work and calling
lessons.idea: Work is a participation in God’s creative work and a way to serve others. It also carries burdens and risks. Faith helps us ask not only “what will pay?” but “whom does this serve?”
lessons.question: What does your work give to others? What does it cost you?
lessons.activity: Write a one-paragraph description of your current or hoped-for work as service: who benefits, what skill it requires and what temptation it brings. Then list one thing you will do this week to do your work “as for the Lord,” and one boundary that protects rest and prayer.
teach: Work is part of God’s plan from the beginning: Adam is placed in the garden “to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work shares in God’s creative action and is a way we serve others and grow in virtue (CCC 2427; Laborem Exercens). Its toil came with the fall; Christ redeems it (Genesis 3:17–19).

The dignity of work rests on the dignity of the worker: work is for the person, not the person for work (CCC 2426–2428). Workers have rights: a just wage, safe conditions, rest, and the freedom to organize (CCC 2433–2436). Employers and employees have duties of justice and honesty.

Jesus worked as a carpenter for thirty years (Mark 6:3). Paul tells the Colossians: “Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord” (3:23–24), and he warns against idleness (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12).

Vocation includes how you spend your days. Ask: What is the good this work serves? Can I do it honestly? Does it leave time for God and family? Idolatry of work and escape from work are both temptations (CCC 2184–2188).
talk: How do you balance ambition and service?
What is a fair wage, and who decides?
How do you keep Sunday different?
quiz: Work has dignity because…|The worker is a person|The state says so|It produces money|It is hard|0|CCC 2428.
The universal destination of goods means…|No private property|God intends the earth’s goods for all|Everything belongs to the state|Everything is free|1|CCC 2402.
Sabbath rest is meant to…|Waste time|Replace prayer|Free us from the idol of work|Make us lazy|2|CCC 2184.
lessons.life: Offer your work to God each morning with the Morning Offering. Notice one way you can serve someone through it.
lessons.saint: Josemaría Escrivá: he taught that ordinary work, done well and for love, can sanctify.
lessons.mem: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord.” (Colossians 3:23)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is your work a job, a career or a calling? What changes if it is a calling?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to write how their work or study can serve others and glorify God.

lessons.title: Money, generosity and justice
lessons.idea: Jesus talks about money more than almost anything. The Church teaches that we are stewards, not owners, and that we have duties of justice and charity to the poor. Generosity frees us.
lessons.question: What is your relationship with money: fear, pride, control, generosity?
lessons.activity: Make a simple one-month budget and decide a percentage for giving. Choose a concrete way to give time as well as money (a soup kitchen, a tutoring program, a visit). After a week, write what you noticed about generosity and fear.
teach: The earth’s goods are meant for everyone: the universal destination of goods (CCC 2402–2406). Private property is legitimate and good but carries a social duty. Jesus warns, “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24) and tells the rich fool’s parable (Luke 12:13–21).

Giving to the poor is not only charity but justice (CCC 2446). The Church asks for a preferential love for the poor (CCC 2443–2449). Sacrificial giving is part of discipleship; tithing, almsgiving and volunteering are habits worth building (Matthew 25:31–46).

Sins against justice include theft, fraud, unjust wages, gambling that harms others, and exploitation (CCC 2408–2414). Debt, consumer culture and the pull of status are spiritual issues as well as financial ones.

Practical steps: make a budget that includes giving, avoid debt that enslaves, support organizations that help the poor with dignity, and consider how your purchases affect workers and creation (CCC 2415–2418).
talk: How much is enough?
How do you give: from the surplus, or sacrificially?
What is the difference between charity and justice?
quiz: A steward is…|A caretaker of what belongs to God|An owner|A landlord|A beggar|0|CCC 2402-2405.
Almsgiving is…|Optional|A work of mercy and a duty of justice|Irrelevant|Only for the rich|1|CCC 2447.
Jesus said we cannot serve…|God and leisure|God and money|God and family|God and wealth and prayer|1|Matthew 6:24.
lessons.life: Give away something this week that costs you: money, time, or an object you like. Do it quietly.
lessons.saint: Martin of Tours: a soldier who cut his cloak in half to clothe a beggar and found it was Christ.
lessons.mem: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)
lessons.hook: Ask for a quick estimate: how much of your income would you give away if you could? Reflect on why.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the universal destination of goods and one practice of generosity.

lessons.title: Catholic social teaching: caring for our neighbor
lessons.idea: The Church’s social teaching rests on the dignity of every person, the common good, solidarity and subsidiarity. It calls Christians to work for justice in family, work, politics and the environment.
lessons.question: Which issue in your community needs attention? How could you respond?
lessons.activity: Pick one social issue in your community (housing, immigration, hunger, the environment, loneliness). Apply three principles to it and write one concrete action you can take (a call, a donation, a volunteer shift, a letter). Share it with a friend and ask them to hold you to it.
teach: Catholic social teaching is the Church’s reflection on society in light of the Gospel, from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Laudato Si’ (2015) (CCC 2419–2425). It is not partisan; it challenges every ideology.

Core principles: the dignity of the human person (CCC 1700–1709); the common good (CCC 1905–1912); subsidiarity (decisions at the lowest competent level, CCC 1883–1885); solidarity (CCC 1939–1942); the preferential option for the poor (CCC 2443–2449); care for creation (CCC 2415–2418).
Micah 6:8 summarizes: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly. Luke 4:18–19 (“good news to the poor”) and Matthew 25 (“I was hungry”) give the pattern. Faith without works is dead (James 2:14–17).

Catholics can disagree on how to apply principles but not on the principles themselves. Good citizens vote, volunteer, speak up and form their conscience with the Church’s teaching (CCC 1913–1917, 2238–2246).
talk: What are non-negotiable (life, dignity) and prudential matters (how to apply)?
How should faith shape how we vote?
What one local action can you commit to?
quiz: Subsidiarity means…|Decisions should be made at the lowest competent level|No government|Higher authorities should do everything|Everything is local|0|CCC 1883.
Which is a principle of Catholic social teaching?|Profit above all|Human dignity|Nationalism|Individualism|1|CCC 1929.
Solidarity means…|Isolation|Sharing the burdens of the whole human family|Charity only|Competition|1|CCC 1939-1940.
lessons.life: Pick one social teaching document from the Papal writings page and read the first ten paragraphs. Tell someone what you learned.
lessons.saint: Frédéric Ozanam: a young scholar who founded the St Vincent de Paul Society at 20 to serve the poor of Paris.
lessons.mem: “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Show a map of a local need. Ask: “Who is missing from our conversations?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name four principles of Catholic social teaching and apply one.

units.title: Hard questions
units.eq: What about suffering, science and other faiths?

lessons.title: Why does God allow suffering?
lessons.idea: Suffering is a mystery. Christians do not claim to have a complete explanation, but they have a Person: God entered suffering in Jesus. Faith offers meaning, presence and hope.
lessons.question: What suffering in your life or the world is hardest for you to square with a good God?
lessons.activity: Write a letter you could give to someone who is suffering (a friend or a past self). Do not explain. Name the pain, say you are with them, offer one practical help, and include a line of Scripture. Then reflect on what the letter shows about what you believe about God.
teach: The Catechism asks the question plainly (CCC 309): if God is good and almighty, why is there evil? No single answer satisfies; “the whole of the Christian faith is the answer” (CCC 309). God is not the author of evil and permits it only to bring a greater good (CCC 311–312).

Some suffering comes from human freedom and sin; some from a creation still “on the way” to its perfection (CCC 310). Job does not receive an explanation; he receives God’s presence (Job 38–42). The right first response to a sufferer is presence, not argument.

Christ does not explain suffering away; he enters it. On the Cross he takes our pain into God (CCC 1521). Paul writes that sufferings are “not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed” (Romans 8:18) and that God works in all things for good (8:28).

Suffering offered with Christ can be redemptive (Colossians 1:24; CCC 1505, 1521), but we never go looking for it, and it must not be used to excuse injustice or abuse. Christians are called to relieve suffering (works of mercy) and to protest evil.
talk: When have you been helped by someone’s presence in suffering?
What are the dangers of easy answers?
How can the Church accompany those who suffer?
quiz: The Church teaches that God permits evil…|And can bring a greater good from it|Because he enjoys it|Because he does not care|Because he is weak|0|CCC 311.
Jesus in suffering…|Enters it and redeems it|Explains it|Avoids it|Is silent|0|CCC 1505.
Redemptive suffering means…|Ignoring pain|Looking for pain|Suffering is good in itself|Suffering united to Christ’s can be offered for others|3|CCC 1521.
lessons.life: Visit or call someone who is suffering this week. Listen more than you speak.
lessons.saint: Josephine Bakhita: enslaved as a child in Sudan, she became a Canossian sister and said, “If I were to meet those who kidnapped me, I would kneel and kiss their hands.”
misc: “A good God would prevent all evil.”
lessons.mem: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” (Romans 8:18)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that real suffering lives in the room. Invite quiet before beginning. Offer to step out.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state what the Church does and does not say about why God allows suffering.

lessons.title: Faith and science
lessons.idea: The Church holds that faith and reason cannot contradict each other, since God is the author of both. She welcomes sound science and warns against both treating Genesis as a science textbook and treating science as the only way to truth.
lessons.question: What science do you love? What conflicts have you felt between science and faith?
lessons.activity: Make two columns: questions science answers best, and questions only philosophy and theology can approach. Put at least five in each. Then read Psalm 19:1–4 and Job 38:4–7 and write how these passages treat creation as a source of wonder rather than a rival explanation.
teach: Faith and science are two ways of seeking truth, and “there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason” (CCC 159). Genesis 1 teaches who made the world, why, and its goodness, in the form of liturgical poetry; it does not compete with cosmology (CCC 282–289, 337).

The Church has no teaching against the big bang or biological evolution as scientific theories. The priest Georges Lemaître proposed the big bang; Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics. What the Church insists on is that creation is good and from God, that each human soul is directly created, and that humans are made in God’s image (CCC 366, 355).

The Galileo case was a failure of judgment on both sides, not a war of religion against science (see Grade 8). Scientism, the claim that only empirical science yields truth, is a philosophical position, not a scientific result.

Questions to hold: What can science tell us? What can it not? Where might theology learn from science (the age of the universe, the interconnectedness of life)? Where does science depend on assumptions it cannot prove (order, intelligibility)?
talk: What can science not answer?
What is the difference between a gap-filling God and the Creator of all?
How could you speak with a skeptic friend?
quiz: Can a Catholic accept evolution?|Only for animals|Never|Yes, as a scientific theory, holding that God creates each soul|Only if it is false|2|CCC 283, 366.
Who proposed the Big Bang theory?|An atheist|A pope|A Catholic priest|A bishop|2|Georges Lemaître.
Genesis 1 teaches…|Detailed science|Nothing|Mythology only|Truths about God and creation in poetic form|3|CCC 289.
lessons.life: Read a short article by a scientist who is a person of faith and note what you learn.
lessons.saint: Albert the Great: patron of scientists, he studied nature and taught that faith and reason work together.
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where did you first hear that faith and science disagree? Who said it?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain how Genesis 1 and science answer different questions.

lessons.title: Other religions, other Christians
lessons.idea: The Church respects what is true and holy in other religions and works for the unity of all Christians. She also proclaims that Jesus Christ is the one Savior of all. Dialogue and mission belong together.
lessons.question: What religions or churches do your friends belong to? What do you share and where do you differ?
lessons.activity: Choose one tradition (Orthodox, Lutheran, Jewish, Muslim, Buddhist, nonbeliever). Read a short, fair description by its own members, then write three things you admire, three differences and one question you would like to ask a friend from that tradition. If possible, invite one to coffee.
teach: The Church holds that Christ is the unique Savior and that the fullness of the means of salvation subsists in the Catholic Church (CCC 816, 846). Yet she “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2; CCC 843), and God can lead those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel to salvation (CCC 847).

Other Christians are in real, if imperfect, communion with the Church through Baptism (CCC 818–819). The Orthodox have valid sacraments and apostolic succession; Protestants share Scripture and Baptism. Unity is Christ’s prayer (John 17:20–23) and the Church works for it through prayer, dialogue and service (CCC 820–822).
Judaism has a unique place: “the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839–840). Anti-Semitism is a sin against the Gospel. Muslims worship the one merciful God (CCC 841).
Dialogue is not relativism: it listens deeply and speaks honestly. Paul in Athens (Acts 17:22–31) begins with what the Athenians already believe, quotes their poets, and then proclaims Christ.
talk: How do you hold conviction and respect together?
What would a Protestant friend find strange about Catholic faith?
What is the difference between dialogue and evangelization?
quiz: Nostra Aetate is about…|Non-Christian religions|Priests|The Bible|The Eucharist|0|Vatican II.
Can non-Christians be saved?|Only baptized|God wills all to be saved; the Church teaches salvation through Christ even for those who sincerely seek him|Only Catholics|Never|1|CCC 847.
Ecumenism seeks…|The end of the Church|Uniformity|Unity of all Christians|Conversion by force|2|CCC 820.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father this week for Christian unity, and invite a friend of another denomination for coffee.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: he prayed at the Western Wall, in a mosque and with leaders of many faiths at Assisi, while preaching Christ.
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Ask about a friend of another faith or none. What do you admire? What do you not understand?
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain how the Church can say Christ is the only Savior and still respect other religions.

units.title: Missionary disciples
units.eq: How do I live this out and share it?

lessons.title: Friendship, community and accountability
lessons.idea: Faith is not meant to be lived alone. Friends, a parish, a small group and a spiritual director help us stay faithful. Real community requires time, honesty and forgiveness.
lessons.question: Who in your life makes it easier to follow Jesus? Who makes it harder?
lessons.activity: Map your current community: who knows you, who challenges you, who you serve. Choose one gap and one concrete step to fill it this month (join a group, ask someone to pray weekly, start a study). Then write a note of thanks to a friend who has helped your faith.
teach: We are made for communion; Genesis 2:18 says “it is not good that the man should be alone.” The Church is the community through which we grow in faith (Acts 2:42–47; Hebrews 10:24–25). Friendship, accountability and shared mission are not extras.
